notes: For \(f:X\to Y\), the notes define \(\Gamma(V,f_*\mathcal F)=\Gamma(f^{-1}V,\mathcal F)\) and ask to check the sheaf axiom. For a one-point target they recover global sections.
statement: If \(f:X\to Y\) is continuous and \(\mathcal F\) a sheaf of sets or abelian groups, then \((f_*\mathcal F)(V)=\mathcal F(f^{-1}V)\), with inherited restrictions, is a sheaf. Inverse images of an open cover cover its inverse image, so the gluing axiom is inherited. For \(Y\) a point its value is \(\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)\).
fate: This is the classical direct-image functor, checked in \citet[Lemma 6.21.1]{stacks2026foundations}; the verification is the elementary exercise posed in the notebook.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established in the stated scope; no open problem is asserted by this item.

title: Sections on the empty open set
notes: The parenthesis says that when \(f^{-1}(V)\) is empty, its set of sections is empty.
statement: For a sheaf of sets, the section set on the empty open is a singleton, by the sheaf axiom for the empty cover. For a sheaf of abelian groups it is the zero group, whose underlying set has one element. Accordingly, \((f_*\mathcal F)(V)\) is terminal, not an empty set, when \(f^{-1}(V)=\varnothing\).
fate: The correction follows immediately from the sheaf definition \citep[Section 6.7]{stacks2026foundations}. The scan repeats the word empty, so this is a faithful mathematical error rather than a translation error.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established in the stated scope; no open problem is asserted by this item.

title: Inverse image characterized by adjunction
notes: The source writes \(f^*\mathcal G\) and a natural bijection \(\operatorname{Hom}(f^*\mathcal G,\mathcal F)=\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal G,f_*\mathcal F)\).
statement: For continuous \(f:X\to Y\), the inverse-image functor on sheaves of sets or abelian groups, denoted \(f^{-1}\), is left adjoint to \(f_*\): \(\operatorname{Hom}_X(f^{-1}\mathcal G,\mathcal F)\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_Y(\mathcal G,f_*\mathcal F)\), naturally in both arguments. This determines inverse image up to canonical isomorphism. For modules on ringed spaces, the usual \(f^*\) additionally tensors with \(\mathcal O_X\).
reconstruction: Modern notation f inverse is used for the functor denoted f star in this topological discussion.
fate: The adjunction is checked in \citet[Section 6.21]{stacks2026foundations}. The distinction between sheaf inverse image and module pullback prevents transferring the bare topological formula to a different category.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established in the stated scope; no open problem is asserted by this item.

title: The inverse-image presheaf and its sheafification
notes: The construction uses the direct limit of \(\mathcal G(V)\) over neighborhoods \(V\supset f(U)\), and asks to show that its associated sheaf is inverse image.
statement: For open \(U\subseteq X\), define \(P(U)=\varinjlim_{V\supseteq f(U)}\mathcal G(V)\), where \(V\) runs through open subsets of \(Y\), ordered by reverse inclusion. Restrictions make \(P\) a presheaf, and \(f^{-1}\mathcal G=aP\). Its stalk at \(x\) is canonically \(\mathcal G_{f(x)}\); sheafification is essential for the adjunction on sheaves.
fate: The construction and stalk statement are \citet[Lemmas 6.21.3--6.21.4 and the following definition]{stacks2026foundations}. The source formula is correct once the open-neighborhood indexing and associated sheaf are retained.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established in the stated scope; no open problem is asserted by this item.

title: Why the two-point pullback presheaf is not a sheaf
notes: Two isolated points map to one point. The construction gives the same value \(\mathcal G\) on each singleton and on the whole two-point space, which the source labels not a sheaf.
statement: Let \(X=\{x_1,x_2\}\) be discrete, \(Y=\{y\}\), and let the sheaf on \(Y\) have value a set \(A\) with at least two elements. The inverse-image presheaf has value \(A\) on every nonempty open, but its value on \(X\) cannot glue arbitrary independent choices at the two points. Its sheafification has \(A\times A\) on \(X\), the locally constant sheaf with fibre \(A\). The example is trivial for a singleton \(A\).
fate: This is the standard distinction between a constant presheaf and constant sheaf, checked in \citet[Example 6.17.4]{stacks2026foundations}. It explains the notebook\textquotesingle s emphatic need for sheafification.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established in the stated scope; no open problem is asserted by this item.

title: Morphisms of sheaves as natural transformations
notes: The footnote defines a morphism by maps on the section sets for every open, commuting with restrictions. One arrow is overwritten and resembles a two-headed arrow.
statement: A morphism \(\phi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G\) over \(X\) is a family \(\phi_U:\mathcal F(U)\to\mathcal G(U)\) such that restriction and \(\phi\) commute for every inclusion of opens. In the group or module category, these are group or module homomorphisms. They need not be bijections; isomorphisms are those with an inverse natural transformation.
fate: This is the standard presheaf and sheaf morphism definition \citep[Definition 6.3.1 and Definition 6.7.1]{stacks2026foundations}. The clear prose and separate right-pointing arrow determine the intended general morphism; the overwritten arrow does not impose invertibility.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established in the stated scope; no open problem is asserted by this item.

title: The universal property of the associated sheaf
notes: The corrected Hom display is followed by a canonical map from the presheaf to its associated object, but the word presheaf is mistakenly repeated for both objects.
statement: For a presheaf \(P\), sheafification is a sheaf \(aP\) with a morphism \(P\to aP\), such that every presheaf morphism \(P\to G\) into a sheaf factors uniquely through \(aP\). Equivalently, \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Sh}}(aP,G)\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{PSh}}(P,G)\) naturally. This makes sheafification left adjoint to inclusion of sheaves into presheaves.
reconstruction: The second object is a sheaf, as required by the heading and Hom universal property; the cancelled preliminary formula is not used.
fate: The exact statement is \citet[Lemma 6.17.3]{stacks2026foundations}; the explicit canonical map in this occurrence supplies the qualification omitted in the earlier same-stalks exercise, 1970-184.7.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established in the stated scope; no open problem is asserted by this item.

title: Sheaves of abelian groups form an abelian category
notes: Lemma 1 says that the category of sheaves of abelian groups on \(X\) is abelian.
statement: For every topological space \(X\), the category \(\operatorname{Sh}(X,\mathbf{Ab})\) is abelian. Kernels are computed on each open, whereas cokernels are obtained by sheafifying the presheaf cokernel; a sequence is exact iff its sequences of stalks are exact. Sections on an arbitrary open need not preserve surjectivity.
fate: This is a basic theorem of sheaf homological algebra, established in the framework of \citet{grothendieck1957homological} and checked in \citet[Lemma 17.3.1, applied to the constant sheaf of integers]{stacks2026foundations}. It is an expository lemma, not a research claim of 1970.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established in the stated scope; no open problem is asserted by this item.

title: Enough injective sheaves
notes: Lemma 2 says that every sheaf embeds in an injective sheaf.
statement: For every topological space \(X\), the abelian category of sheaves of abelian groups has enough injectives. Thus every sheaf admits an injective resolution. One construction embeds each stalk into an injective abelian group and maps the sheaf into the product of the corresponding direct-image sheaves at the points.
fate: This is the classical existence theorem used by \citet{grothendieck1957homological}; the pointwise construction is checked in \citet[Section 19.4]{stacks2026foundations}. The claim is about abelian-group sheaves, not an unqualified assertion for sheaves of sets.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established in the stated scope; no open problem is asserted by this item.

title: Cohomology as derived global sections
notes: The notes call \(\Gamma\) left semiexact and define \(H^i\) as its derived functors, contrasting them with Cech calculations.
statement: Global sections \(\Gamma(X,-):\operatorname{Sh}(X,\mathbf{Ab})\to\mathbf{Ab}\) are left exact. For an injective resolution \(\mathcal F\to I^\bullet\), define \(H^q(X,\mathcal F)=H^q(\Gamma(X,I^\bullet))=R^q\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)\). The resulting groups are independent of the resolution up to canonical isomorphism and have the usual long exact sequence.
fate: This is the derived-functor definition of sheaf cohomology from \citet{grothendieck1957homological}; its precise formulation is checked in \citet[Section 20.2]{stacks2026foundations}. The notebook correctly separates the abstract definition from methods of computing it.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established in the stated scope; no open problem is asserted by this item.

title: Cech cohomology on acyclic covers
notes: The final lines mention a topology basis with vanishing Cech groups and say that actual cohomology agrees with Cech computations on acyclic covers.
statement: Let \(\mathcal U=\{U_\alpha\}\) cover \(X\), and let \(\mathcal F\) be an abelian sheaf. If every nonempty finite intersection \(U_{\alpha_0}\cap\cdots\cap U_{\alpha_p}\) is \(\mathcal F\)-acyclic in positive derived-functor degrees, then \(\check H^q(\mathcal U,\mathcal F)\simeq H^q(X,\mathcal F)\). A basis criterion using Cech vanishing must in addition specify covers cofinal under refinement and stability of their intersections; one unspecified vanishing display is insufficient.
reconstruction: The stated acyclic-cover theorem is a precise sufficient interpretation; the notebook does not record every assumption of its separate basis criterion.
fate: The precise cover comparison and basis criterion are \citet[Section 20.11, especially Lemmas 20.11.6 and 20.11.9]{stacks2026foundations}. For quasi-coherent sheaves, affine intersections give the familiar application \citep[Lemma 30.2.6]{stacks2026foundations}, building on \citet{grothendieck1957homological}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established in the stated scope; no open problem is asserted by this item.

title: Solvability of an unspecified elliptic system
notes: The source says \ru{Эллипт. сист. 2-го порядка} on a manifold \ru{без младших членов}, then asks whether it has solutions.
statement: A determinate solvability question requires the operator or nonlinear system, the domain and boundary conditions, the right-hand side, the solution class and the exclusion or inclusion of trivial solutions. Absence of lower-order terms does not supply these missing data. For a homogeneous linear system, zero is always a solution.
fate: Targeted English and Russian searches combining Gelfand, elliptic systems without lower-order terms and parity of solutions yielded no exact match. \citet[Section 2, pp.~119--123]{gelfand1960elliptic} studies homotopy invariants and indices of specified elliptic boundary problems, and discusses operators without lower-order terms. It is thematic background; it does not determine the missing operator or make the fragment an index-theorem question.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: the mathematical question is underdetermined; no solved or open status is assigned.

title: The unexplained Laplace comparison
notes: The next sentence says that for the Laplace operator it is known that there are no solutions.
statement: Without the omitted qualifier, this is not a valid general statement about harmonic functions: constants solve the homogeneous scalar Laplace equation, and zero solves homogeneous Dirichlet data. The source may intend a nontriviality or boundary requirement, but it supplies none that can be reconstructed uniquely.
fate: The Laplace sentence cannot be identified with a particular nonexistence theorem from the available context. Its failure as a bare statement does not license attributing a specific false theorem to the speaker.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: an essential condition is missing; the intended nonexistence assertion remains unidentified.

title: Parity of solutions and an unspecified topological principle
notes: The remaining lines mention the number of solutions modulo two, that in principle the maximum is topology, and a zero-th solution of the Dirichlet problem.
statement: To define a parity count one needs a finite or suitably compact zero-dimensional solution set, or an appropriate proper Fredholm or finite-dimensional degree construction, with regularity or multiplicity conventions. None is stated. The words topology and Dirichlet do not determine such an invariant or establish its stability.
fate: \citet[Section 2, especially pp.~120--123]{gelfand1960elliptic} gives a related topological research programme, including the Fredholm index as kernel dimension minus adjoint-kernel dimension. This is not a count of individual solutions modulo two. No exact parity theorem was located in the checked sources; the notebook direction remains unidentified.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: neither a parity theorem nor a well-posed parity problem can be extracted without additional archival information.

title: Regularity is minimal centralizer dimension
notes: A regular element is said to have centralizer of rank \(n-1\); the group is described as complex semisimple, of type \(A_n\) or \(D_n\).
statement: For a connected complex semisimple algebraic group of rank \(r\), an element is regular when \(\dim Z_G(g)=r\), the minimal possible centralizer dimension. It is dimension, not rank of the centralizer, that detects regularity. In \(SL_n\), \(r=n-1\), whereas a group of type \(A_n\) has rank \(n\); the notebook leaves its integer convention unresolved.
reconstruction: The group rank r replaces the unspecified matrix-size or Dynkin-index convention.
fate: This is the definition in \citet[p.~49]{steinberg1965regular}, published in 1965. The mismatch of centralizer rank and dimension is a faithful source error; replacing the ambiguous n by rank r makes the assertion precise.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established in the stated scope; no open problem is asserted by this item.

title: Subregular centralizers have dimension rank plus two
notes: The source assigns a subregular element centralizer dimension \(n-2\) and adds two coinciding eigenvalues.
statement: In the usual complex semisimple setting, subregular elements have centralizer dimension \(r+2\), the next dimension after regularity. For a semisimple element of \(SL_n\) with exactly one eigenvalue of multiplicity two and all other eigenvalues distinct, the centralizer dimension is \(4+(n-2)-1=n+1=(n-1)+2\). This eigenvalue description is a type-A example, not a uniform definition for type D.
reconstruction: The standard subregular dimension and the checked type-A example are given separately; the archival n minus two is not retained as a valid centralizer formula.
fate: The minimum-dimension characterization and structure of irregular elements are part of the classical setting of \citet[Sections 1 and 5]{steinberg1965regular}. The explicit block-centralizer calculation verifies the type-A correction directly; no later singularity theorem is inserted into the fragment.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established in the stated scope; no open problem is asserted by this item.

title: Regularity and smoothness of the adjoint quotient
notes: The map \(G\to H/W\), with \(H\) a Cartan subgroup and \(W\) its Weyl group, is followed by regular element if and only if the map is regular there.
statement: For a connected simply connected complex semisimple group \(G\) of rank \(r\), the adjoint quotient \(\chi:G\to H/W\simeq\mathbb A^r\) is smooth at \(g\) iff \(g\) is regular. Equivalently the differentials of its fundamental character coordinates are independent there. Here regular for the map must mean nonsingular or submersive, not merely algebraic regularity, which holds everywhere.
reconstruction: Simply connectedness and the smooth/submersive meaning of regular map are explicit sufficient hypotheses and terminology.
fate: \citet[Theorem 1.5, Theorem 8.1 and Remark 8.7]{steinberg1965regular} supplies the exact criterion and its simply connected qualification. This verifies the identifiable statement, but does not prove that Steinberg is the unnamed particular work reported in 1970; no stronger bibliographical identification is made.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established in the stated scope; no open problem is asserted by this item.

title: Monochromatic subspaces over a finite field
notes: The notes fix \(F_q\), integers \(\ell<k\), and assert existence of \(N\) such that a partition of the \(\ell\)-subspaces of \(F_q^N\) contains a \(k\)-subspace whose \(\ell\)-subspaces lie in one class.
statement: For every prime power \(q\), every integers \(r\geq1\) and \(1\leq\ell<k\), there is \(N=N(q,r,\ell,k)\) such that every map \(c:\operatorname{Gr}_{\ell}(F_q^N)\to\{1,\ldots,r\}\) is constant on \(\operatorname{Gr}_{\ell}(E)\) for some \(k\)-dimensional \(E\leq F_q^N\).
reconstruction: The explicit finite color parameter \(r\), and its position before \(N\), are supplied. Without that order of quantifiers, coloring every subspace differently disproves the literal reading.
fate: Established by \citet[abstract and pp.~119--120]{grahamleebrothschild1972ramsey}; the announcement appeared in January 1972. The current search did not establish an earlier public circulation date.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Solved; the finite-field, fixed-finite-color formulation is essential.

title: The line case and its projective interpretation
notes: \ru{Для \(\ell=1\) доказана.} A projective line is sought in one of two classes of projective points.
statement: For fixed \(q,r,k\), sufficiently large projective space \(\mathbf P^{N-1}(F_q)\), colored with \(r\) colors, contains a monochromatic projective \((k-1)\)-space. Vector-space dimension is one greater than projective dimension.
fate: This is the \(\ell=1\) specialization of \citet[abstract]{grahamleebrothschild1972ramsey}. The notebook itself attests that this specialization was already known to the seminar; this run did not identify the exact earlier announcement used by Gelfand.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established special case; the archival assertion about prior proof is preserved without assigning an unverified pre-1970 reference.

title: The sheaf associated to a module
notes: The notes recall module localization by fractions and set \(\Gamma(U_f,\mathcal F_M)=M_f\); listeners are asked to verify that this is a sheaf.
statement: For a commutative ring \(A\) and any \(A\)-module \(M\), the localization rule \(D(f)\mapsto M_f\), with canonical restrictions, satisfies the basis sheaf condition and determines a unique sheaf \(\widetilde M\). Its stalk at \(\mathfrak p\) is \(M_{\mathfrak p}\), and its global sections are \(M\). Fractions satisfy \(m/s=m^{\prime}/s^{\prime}\) iff some \(t\in S\) kills \(s^{\prime}m-sm^{\prime}\).
fate: The construction is the established affine module-sheaf construction, checked in \citet[Lemma 26.5.4 and Lemma 26.7.1]{stacks2026foundations}. It extends the localization material of 1970-184.4--5 to arbitrary modules.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established in the stated scope; no open problem is asserted by this item.

title: Equivalent definitions of quasi-coherence
notes: The initial definition uses local cokernels of free sheaves; the second uses local isomorphisms to \(\mathcal F_M\). An exercise asks for equivalence.
statement: For a sheaf of modules on a scheme, the following local conditions are equivalent: it is associated to a module on an affine open neighborhood; it admits a presentation there by direct sums of copies of the structure sheaf. Arbitrary modules admit free presentations, and localization is exact, so a module presentation sheafifies to a local free presentation; conversely an affine free-sheaf map comes from the corresponding module map.
fate: This is \citet[Definition 17.10.1 and Lemmas 17.10.5, 26.7.1 and 26.7.4]{stacks2026foundations}, already implicit in \citet{grothendieck1960ega1}. The equivalence is an expository exercise, not a new problem of 1970.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established in the stated scope; no open problem is asserted by this item.

title: Free presentations need not have finite rank
notes: The proposed solution displays \(A^m\to A^n\to M\) and \(\mathcal O^m\to\mathcal O^n\to\mathcal F_M\), then reverses the construction by taking sections.
statement: For arbitrary \(M\), use an exact sequence \(A^{(I)}\to A^{(J)}\to M\to0\) with possibly infinite sets \(I,J\), and the corresponding sheaf sequence. Finite \(m,n\) are justified when \(M\) is finitely presented, a stronger assumption than quasi-coherence. In the converse, form the cokernel of the module map and identify its sheaf locally; do not assume right exactness of arbitrary section functors as a premise.
reconstruction: The letters m and n are replaced by index sets for the unrestricted theorem. The proof order avoids using the desired affine exactness circularly.
fate: Exactness of the associated-sheaf functor and the free-presentation characterization are checked in \citet[Lemma 26.5.4 and Section 26.7]{stacks2026foundations}. The arbitrary-index convention had been stated explicitly in the 7 September lecture but is suppressed in this diagram.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established in the stated scope; no open problem is asserted by this item.

title: Every quasi-coherent sheaf on an affine is a module sheaf
notes: The main theorem says every quasi-coherent \(\mathcal F\) on \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) has the form \(\mathcal F_M\); its proof sets \(M=\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)\).
statement: For \(X=\operatorname{Spec}A\) and quasi-coherent \(\mathcal F\), the canonical morphism \(\widetilde{\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)}\to\mathcal F\) is an isomorphism. Thus the local module presentations globalize uniquely up to the canonical module identification; no finite-generation, Noetherian or separatedness hypothesis beyond affineness is required.
fate: This is the affine equivalence of \citet[Lemma 26.7.5]{stacks2026foundations}, first introduced in record 184 and classical by \citet{grothendieck1960ega1}. The choice of the global-section module is part of the theorem, rather than an arbitrary existence assertion.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established in the stated scope; no open problem is asserted by this item.

title: Quasi-compactness of affine spectra
notes: The proof recalls that every affine scheme is quasi-compact, with a parenthesis about absence of separation, and chooses a finite subcover.
statement: Every open cover of \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) has a finite subcover. Refine to principal opens \(D(f_i)\); covering means the \(f_i\) generate the unit ideal, so a finite sum \(\sum a_if_i=1\) selects a finite subcover. This topological quasi-compactness does not assert that the underlying space is Hausdorff.
fate: This is checked in \citet[Lemma 10.17.8]{stacks2026foundations}. The parenthesis distinguishes quasi-compactness from a Hausdorff compactness convention; it does not deny the scheme-theoretic separatedness of affine schemes.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established in the stated scope; no open problem is asserted by this item.

title: The canonical localization map and clearing denominators
notes: After choosing a finite cover with \(\mathcal F|_{D(f_i)}=\widetilde M_i\), the notes construct \(M_f\to\Gamma(D(f),\mathcal F)\) because \(1/f\) is a section of the structure sheaf there.
statement: For any module sheaf \(\mathcal F\), restriction \(M=\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)\to\Gamma(D(f),\mathcal F)\) factors canonically through \(M_f\), since multiplication by \(f\) is invertible on \(D(f)\). For quasi-coherent \(\mathcal F\) on affine \(X\), a finite principal-open cover with local module descriptions permits a common power of \(f\) to clear all denominators and compatibility defects; this proves the map is an isomorphism and hence the main theorem.
reconstruction: The missing remainder of the proof is summarized using the standard denominator-clearing argument; the source itself stops after defining the natural map.
fate: The localization identities and proof of global recovery are checked in \citet[Lemmas 26.7.1--26.7.5]{stacks2026foundations}. The construction of the map is valid before quasi-coherence; its being an isomorphism uses quasi-coherence and the finite cover.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established in the stated scope; no open problem is asserted by this item.

title: Quadratic pairs
notes: \((G,M)\): \(M\) is a faithful irreducible \(F_p\)-representation and \(G\) is generated by elements satisfying \(M(g-1)^2=0\).
statement: A quadratic pair consists of a nontrivial finite group \(G\), an odd prime \(p\), and a faithful irreducible finite-dimensional \(F_pG\)-module \(M\) such that \(G=\langle Q\rangle\), where \(Q=\{g\ne1:(g-I)^2M=0\}\). Such generators have Jordan blocks of sizes at most two, with at least one size-two block.
reconstruction: Finiteness of the group, finite-dimensionality, exclusion of the identity as a generator, and the odd-prime convention are supplied from the published definition.
fate: Thompson's Nice ICM lecture circulated in 1970 and appeared in 1971; see \citet[p.~375, Definition]{thompson1971quadratic}. The later treatment is \citet[Hypothesis~1.0]{chermak2004quadratic}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: The central-product and Lie-type classification for odd primes at least five
notes: For \(p>5\), the notes say that \(G\) is only a classical group, listing \(S,O\), and adding \ru{кроме \(E_8\)}.
statement: For a quadratic pair with \(p\geq5\), the structural conclusion involves a central product of perfect groups with simple central quotients and a corresponding tensor decomposition of the module. In the quasisimple case the simple quotient is of Lie type in characteristic \(p\), from the families listed in Thompson's theorem, including exceptional families \(G_2,F_4,E_6,E_7\), but excluding \(E_8\). It is not a conclusion that \(G\) itself is a single classical simple group.
reconstruction: The central-product reduction and exceptional Lie types are restored from the checked Thompson theorem; the literal classical-group slogan is not retained as a theorem.
fate: \citet[p.~375, Central product theorem and Main theorem]{thompson1971quadratic} gives precisely the missing structural qualifications. It was reported at Nice before the October seminar, although the proceedings were printed in 1971.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established structural classification; the notebook's word classical and its omission of central products are not literal equivalents of the theorem.

title: The small-characteristic continuation of quadratic-pair theory
notes: \ru{Остались хар-ки 2 и 3.}
statement: The definite odd-characteristic continuation is to classify faithful irreducible quadratic pairs over \(F_3\). The characteristic-two phrase does not specify what additional restrictions distinguish the intended problem: in characteristic two every involution satisfies \((g-I)^2=0\).
reconstruction: The characteristic-three problem is separated from the underspecified characteristic-two slogan; no claim of solving every characteristic-two classification problem is made.
fate: For characteristic three, \citet[Theorems~A--B; introduction]{chermak2004quadratic} treats the component case using the finite-simple-group classification and points to the earlier component-free treatment. The opened preprint is dated February 2002; publication was 2004. Its introduction explains that the original program was displaced by a different route to the finite-simple-group classification.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: The odd-characteristic quadratic-pair program has a classification-based treatment. The unqualified characteristic-two slogan is not assigned an exact solved theorem.

title: The rootless even unimodular lattice in dimension twenty-four
notes: Kirillov describes \(L\subset\mathbf R^{24}\) with covolume one, integral pairings, even squared norms, and minimum squared norm four, and says it is unique.
statement: Up to Euclidean isometry there is a unique positive-definite even unimodular lattice of rank 24 with no norm-two vectors: the Leech lattice. Its minimum over nonzero vectors is four. The zero vector must be excluded from the minimum.
reconstruction: Evenness, unimodularity, positive definiteness, rank 24, and absence of roots delimit the standard uniqueness statement.
fate: \citet[Theorem~1.1 and proof]{brouwerleech} reproduces Conway's uniqueness proof. The original 1969 characterization is identified there; this is prior work, not an unpublished seminar conjecture.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established; uniqueness is up to isometry and the minimum is over nonzero lattice vectors.
speaker: A. A. Kirillov

title: Conway's simple group requires a central quotient
notes: The notes describe another finite simple group, Conway's, as the automorphism group of this lattice.
statement: For the Leech lattice \(\Lambda\), \(\operatorname{Aut}(\Lambda)\) contains the central inversion \(-I\). The simple Conway group is \(\mathrm{Co}_1=\operatorname{Aut}(\Lambda)/\{\pm I\}\), not the full automorphism group.
reconstruction: The central quotient by \(\{\pm I\}\) separates the full automorphism group from the simple Conway group.
fate: The lattice automorphism group and its order occur in \citet[Theorem~1.1]{brouwerleech}; \citet[introduction, pp.~2--3]{chermak2004quadratic} explicitly identifies it as \(2\cdot\mathrm{Co}_1\). These confirm the missing central quotient independently of the notebook.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established after inserting the quotient by central inversion.
speaker: A. A. Kirillov

title: Divisibility of the signature for even unimodular lattices
notes: \ru{Сигнатура дел. на 8 у полож. опр. форм.}
statement: An even unimodular positive-definite integral lattice has rank, hence signature, divisible by eight. Positivity alone is insufficient: a one-dimensional positive form has signature one.
reconstruction: The surrounding even-unimodular lattice context is imposed; the unrestricted positive-definite-form reading is false.
fate: The lattice hypotheses in the surrounding passage supply the intended scope; \citet[Theorem~1.2(i)]{brouwerleech} states rank divisibility for even unimodular lattices.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Classical theorem under evenness and unimodularity; false if read as an assertion about all positive-definite forms.

title: The proposed point-supported counterexample
notes: A sheaf is said to have fibre \(A\) at one point \(x\in\operatorname{Spec}A\), zero elsewhere, and sections \(A\) exactly on opens containing \(x\); it is called non-quasi-coherent.
statement: The formula defines a skyscraper sheaf of abelian groups. To make it an \(\mathcal O_X\)-module one must specify an \(\mathcal O_{X,x}=A_{\mathfrak p}\)-module structure on its value. Moreover, its stalk support is the closure of \(\{x\}\), so the description of its fibres requires \(x\) to be closed. A usual skyscraper \(i_*\kappa(x)\) at a closed point is quasi-coherent, and therefore does not give the claimed counterexample.
fate: No exact well-posed non-quasi-coherent example is identifiable from these data. The affine module/sheaf correspondence in \citet[affine case]{serre1955coherent} explains why the standard closed-point skyscraper cannot support the claim. The missing action cannot be supplied from the word fibre alone.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: The intended example remains unidentified from the source; this is an identification limit, not a presently open theorem.

title: Localization kills elements annihilated by the denominator
notes: The boxed margin calculation is \(fm=0\Rightarrow m/f=mf/f^2=0\).
statement: For any commutative ring \(A\), \(A\)-module \(M\), and \(f\in A\), an element \(m/f^r\in M_f\) is zero if and only if \(f^Nm=0\) for some \(N\geq0\). The displayed calculation is the case \(fm=0\).
fate: This elementary localization fact underlies the denominator-clearing proof of affine acyclicity, given in \citet[Lemma~30.2.1]{stacks2026affine}. It is not an injectivity assertion for \(M\to M_f\).
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: A globally defined rational expression on an affine variety is polynomial modulo its ideal
notes: If \(P/Q\) is defined everywhere on the subvariety corresponding to \(I\subset\mathbf C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), then \(P/Q=R\pmod I\) for a polynomial \(R\).
statement: Let \(A=\mathbf C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), and suppose \(Q\) has no zero on \(V(I)\). Then \((I,Q)=A\) by the Nullstellensatz; hence \(Q\) is invertible in \(A/I\) and \(P/Q\) is the image of a polynomial. More generally, the ring of global regular functions on the affine scheme \(\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)\) is \(A/I\).
reconstruction: For the single-fraction proof, defined means that the chosen denominator \(Q\) is nowhere zero, not merely that a removable singularity can be canceled locally.
fate: This is a standard affine consequence of the module/sheaf correspondence in \citet[affine case]{serre1955coherent}; the explicit Nullstellensatz proof is resumed on P000309.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: Ideal sheaves and the closed affine subscheme
notes: An ideal \(J\subset A\) gives \(\mathcal F_J\subset\mathcal O_X\); the quotient sheaf is associated with \(A/J\), and its support is the subvariety.
statement: Sheafification on \(X=\operatorname{Spec}A\) is exact. Thus \(0\to\widetilde J\to\mathcal O_X\to\widetilde{A/J}\to0\) is exact and \(\widetilde{A/J}=i_*\mathcal O_{\operatorname{Spec}(A/J)}\) for the closed immersion \(i\). Prime ideals, not only complex closed points, are included in \(X\).
fate: Classical affine scheme theory, as in \citet[affine case]{serre1955coherent}; arbitrary-ring affine acyclicity is verified in \citet[Lemma~30.2.2]{stacks2026affine}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: Gluing a supported section before taking global sections
notes: The notes glue \(P/Q\) on the locus where \(Q\ne0\) to zero on the complement of the subvariety.
statement: In \(\widetilde{A/I}\), which vanishes away from \(V(I)\), the two sections agree on the overlap. Their glued section over all of \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) lies in \(\Gamma(X,\widetilde{A/I})=A/I\). This gluing must be performed in the quotient sheaf, not in \(\mathcal O_X\).
reconstruction: The sheaf in which the two local sections are compared is made explicit.
fate: The argument is a concrete use of the affine correspondence, not a new extension theorem; compare \citet[affine case]{serre1955coherent}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: Recovering a quasi-coherent sheaf from its global module
notes: A presentation by sums of \(\mathcal O_X\) is compared with the corresponding module presentation, concluding \(\mathcal F=\mathcal F_M\).
statement: For every affine scheme \(X=\operatorname{Spec}A\), the functors \(M\mapsto\widetilde M\) and \(\mathcal F\mapsto\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)\) are inverse equivalences between \(A\)-modules and quasi-coherent \(\mathcal O_X\)-modules. Presentations can use arbitrary direct sums; finite presentations require the corresponding finite-presentation hypothesis.
fate: The coherent affine case predates the seminar in \citet{serre1955coherent}; the standard arbitrary-ring formulation is compatible with \citet[Lemma~30.2.2 and its preceding section]{stacks2026affine}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: The quasi-local spin algebra
notes: Two-dimensional spaces \(H_i\), tensor products \(H_I\), matrix rings \(\mathcal A(I)\), and inclusions by tensoring with the identity are introduced.
statement: For finite \(I\subset\mathbf Z\), set \(H_I=\bigotimes_{i\in I}\mathbf C^2\) and \(\mathcal A(I)=B(H_I)\). The compatible embeddings \(a\mapsto a\otimes1\) give the unital UHF \(C^*\)-algebra \(\mathcal A=\overline{\bigcup_I\mathcal A(I)}^{\|\cdot\|}\). In particular \(\dim H_I=2^{|I|}\), not \(2|I|\).
fate: This uniformly hyperfinite setup is used in \citet[section~2]{powers1967representations}. It was standard before the lecture.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: States and local density matrices
notes: A positive functional \(\varphi\) with \(\varphi(1)=1\) restricts to \(\operatorname{Tr}(a\rho_I)\) on each local matrix algebra.
statement: A state is a positive complex-linear functional of norm one. Every restriction to \(\mathcal A(I)\) has a unique density matrix \(\rho_I\geq0\), \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho_I=1\); consistency means \(\operatorname{Tr}_{J\setminus I}\rho_J=\rho_I\) for \(I\subset J\). Conversely a compatible family defines a state on \(\mathcal A\).
fate: The finite-dimensional trace representation and the UHF state construction are the framework of \citet[section~2]{powers1967representations}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: Product-diagonal states and cylinder measures
notes: In a fixed sitewise basis the eigenvalues of the density matrices are treated as joint probabilities.
statement: Choose an orthonormal basis at each site. Compatible density matrices diagonal in all resulting tensor bases are equivalent to probability measures on \(\{1,2\}^{\mathbf Z}\). For a finite word \(\alpha\), its probability is \(\varphi(\bigotimes_{i\in I}|e^i_{\alpha_i}\rangle\langle e^i_{\alpha_i}|)\). It is not the value of \(\varphi\) on a tensor product of vectors.
reconstruction: Rank-one projections replace the notebook's vector expression so that the state is applied to an element of its algebra.
fate: This is the commutative cylinder-measure construction inside the diagonal subalgebra of the UHF algebra. Product states are examined in \citet[section~4]{powers1967representations}. Record 197 attempts a broader commutation criterion, which fails without additional hypotheses.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: Finite-volume Gibbs functionals
notes: A translated nearest-neighbor operator is summed to form a Hamiltonian, and normalized traces of \(ae^{-\beta H_n}\) are taken.
statement: For a self-adjoint nearest-neighbor interaction \(h\in\mathcal A(\{0,1\})\), real finite \(\beta\), and a finite interval \(\Lambda\), put \(H_\Lambda=\sum_{\{j,j+1\}\subset\Lambda}\tau_j(h)\). The state is \(\varphi_\Lambda(a)=\operatorname{Tr}(ae^{-\beta H_\Lambda})/\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H_\Lambda})\) on \(\mathcal A(\Lambda)\).
reconstruction: Self-adjointness of the local interaction, real finite inverse temperature, and the free finite-volume boundary convention are supplied to make the normalized trace a state.
fate: The finite-range spin-chain Gibbs construction is treated in \citet{araki1969gibbs}. Positivity requires a self-adjoint Hamiltonian; no arbitrary matrix \(h\) suffices.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: The one-dimensional Gibbs limit
notes: The notes assert convergence \(\varphi_n(a)\to\varphi(a)\) for every quasi-local observable.
statement: For a translation-invariant finite-range self-adjoint interaction on a one-dimensional quantum spin lattice, the finite-temperature thermodynamic limit with the usual free finite-volume boundary convention exists. The resulting state is primary; the finite-dimensional local state spaces and finite interaction range are part of the assertion.
reconstruction: The hypotheses are those of the identified Araki theorem; the assertion is not extended beyond finite-range one-dimensional quantum spin systems.
fate: \citet[abstract]{araki1969gibbs}, published in 1969, states existence of the infinite-volume primary Gibbs state, before Sinai's lecture. This is an exact match for the finite-range one-dimensional situation, not an assertion about arbitrary dimension or long-range interactions.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established for the stated one-dimensional finite-range finite-temperature system.

title: The analogy with Markov chains
notes: The Gibbs construction is called a noncommutative analogue of Markov chains.
statement: The nearest-neighbor energy resembles a one-step Markov model with Gibbs weights. For noncommuting quantum interactions this analogy alone does not assert a conditional-independence identity, a transition operator, or the modern quantum Markov property.
fate: \citet{araki1969gibbs} supplies a rigorous quantum Gibbs theory. No exact quantum Markov theorem is stated or proved in the notebook passage; the publication match is thematic.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: A useful structural analogy, with no additional Markov theorem inferred.

title: The GNS Hilbert space and generated von Neumann algebra
notes: \((a,b)=\varphi(b^*a)\); factor by null vectors, complete, and let the algebra act by left multiplication.
statement: Let \(N_\varphi=\{a:\varphi(a^*a)=0\}\). Complete \(\mathcal A/N_\varphi\) in the inner product \(\langle[a],[b]\rangle=\varphi(b^*a)\). Left multiplication gives a bounded representation \(\pi_\varphi\), since \(\|\pi_\varphi(x)\|\leq\|x\|\), and \(M_\varphi=\pi_\varphi(\mathcal A)^{\prime\prime}\). The null space is a left ideal; it need not be a two-sided ideal.
fate: The construction and factor representations are used throughout \citet{powers1967representations}; the notebook cites the classical Gelfand--Naimark tradition. This is prior foundational theory.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: When is the GNS algebra a factor, and what type occurs?
notes: The notes ask when the generated ring is a factor and emphasize factors of type III.
statement: The factor question is whether \(Z(M_\varphi)=\mathbf C1\). It is separate from the type of a factor. States of the same UHF algebra can yield type I, type II, or type III factors; the phrase principally type III is a motivation, not a theorem about every state.
fate: \citet[Theorem~2.5]{powers1967representations} gives the factor criterion later explained in record 200; section~4 exhibits the different types for product states. In particular the tracial product state yields type \(\mathrm{II}_1\).
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: The factor criterion and important examples were established before the seminar; no universal type-III assertion is valid.

title: Vanishing of higher cohomology on an affine scheme
notes: For an affine scheme \(X\) and a quasi-coherent sheaf \(\mathcal F\), \(H^q(X,\mathcal F)=0\), \(q>0\).
statement: For every commutative ring \(A\) and every \(A\)-module \(M\), \[H^q(\operatorname{Spec}A,\widetilde M)=0\qquad(q>0).\] Neither Noetherianity nor finite generation of \(M\) is required.
fate: The coherent algebraic-geometric theorem is in \citet{serre1955coherent}. The exact arbitrary-ring formulation and proof are \citet[Lemma~30.2.2]{stacks2026affine}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: The Nullstellensatz proof of Bernstein's rational-function example
notes: For generators \(F_i\) of the ideal and a nowhere-zero \(Q\), find \(L_0Q+\sum_iL_iF_i=P\).
statement: If \((Q,F_1,\ldots,F_r)\) has no common zero over an algebraically closed field, it is the unit ideal. Multiplying a representation of one by \(P\) produces the displayed identity and \(P/Q\equiv L_0\pmod I\).
fate: This proves the single-denominator instance of 1970-194.1 by elementary affine algebra; it does not need the cohomology theorem subsequently being proved. Compare \citet[affine case]{serre1955coherent}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: The localization Čech complex
notes: For \(X_i=D(f_i)\) covering \(\operatorname{Spec}A\), cochains have components in \(M_{f_{i_0}\cdots f_{i_q}}\), with alternating restriction differential.
statement: Choose \(f_1,\ldots,f_r\) generating the unit ideal. The augmented complex starts \(M\to\prod_i M_{f_i}\to\prod_{i<j}M_{f_if_j}\to\cdots\). With increasing indices, \((dc)_{i_0\cdots i_{q+1}}=\sum_{s=0}^{q+1}(-1)^s c_{i_0\cdots\widehat{i_s}\cdots i_{q+1}}\) after restriction.
fate: \citet[Lemma~30.2.1]{stacks2026affine} gives exactness for this finite principal cover and identifies the finite localization argument.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: Alternating cochains and the failed single-chart contraction
notes: The notes pass to skew-symmetric cochains; for a one-cocycle they first try one distinguished index, then note that \(m_{1i}\) may have an unwanted denominator.
statement: The normalized alternating Čech complex computes the same cohomology as the full ordered-index complex. A contraction based on a fixed chart is valid after localizing where that chart covers everything, but \(m_{1i}\in M_{f_1f_i}\) need not already lie in \(M_{f_i}\). The latter obstruction invalidates a global single-chart primitive.
fate: The localization contraction in \citet[proof of Lemma~30.2.1]{stacks2026affine} makes precisely this distinction. The notebook records the failed step as part of a proof search, not a completed proof.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: Uniform denominator clearing and a partition of unity in the ring
notes: Write \(m_{ij}=\bar m_{ij}/(f_i^Nf_j^N)\), choose \(\sum_iL_if_i^N=1\), and sum over \(i\).
statement: After increasing a common power enough to clear all denominators and all finitely many cocycle equalities, a ring identity \(\sum_i L_if_i^N=1\) gives a primitive. For the convention \(m_{ij}=n_i-n_j\), one can set \(n_i=\sum_k L_k f_k^N m_{ik}\) in \(M_{f_i}\), after the clearing step. Equality in a localization may require an additional power before it holds in an earlier module.
fate: This is the standard algebraic proof behind \citet[Lemma~30.2.1]{stacks2026affine}. The corrected formula removes an extraneous denominator from one displayed intermediate equality on P000311; the later lines of the manuscript have the intended sum.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: Bernstein's annihilator proof of affine acyclicity
notes: Each class is killed by a power of every \(f_i\), and those powers still generate the unit ideal.
statement: Localizing the Čech complex at \(f_i\) makes its cover contain the whole affine scheme and hence contracts it. For any given higher-cohomology class \(c\), there are powers with \(f_i^{N_i}c=0\). Finiteness of the cover gives a common \(N\); since \((f_1^N,\ldots,f_r^N)=A\), one obtains \(c=0\).
fate: \citet[proof of Lemma~30.2.1]{stacks2026affine} presents the same localization-to-vanishing mechanism. The argument is valid for arbitrary modules.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.
speaker: I. N. Bernstein

title: Tensor-product local systems and compatible density operators
notes: The first display has \(H_I=\bigoplus_{i\in I}H_i\), but the basis, algebra embeddings and partial trace formulas use tensor products.
statement: The intended local Hilbert space is \(H_I=\bigotimes_{i\in I}H_i\), with \(\mathcal A(J)=\mathcal A(I)\otimes\mathcal A(J\setminus I)\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}_{J\setminus I}\rho_J=\rho_I\). This restates 1970-195.1--2.
fate: The UHF framework in \citet[section~2]{powers1967representations} fixes the notation. The direct-sum sign is a faithful manuscript slip, not a valid alternative construction.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: Commuting finite marginals need not have a common product eigenbasis
notes: A state is called of measure type when all embedded \(\rho_I\) commute. The next page asserts a common tensor basis of eigenvectors of the one-site densities, explicitly noting that the argument is obvious for simple spectra.
statement: Product diagonality implies commutation. The converse is valid if every one-site density has simple spectrum: commuting with each local one-site density forces diagonalization in their product basis. Without that hypothesis, pairwise commutation of all embedded finite marginals is insufficient, even when every finite marginal is strictly positive.
reconstruction: The notebook's commutation definition and the stronger product-diagonal property are kept separate. A repair by simple one-site spectra is explicitly conditional.
fate: The implication fails by the faithful Bell-pair construction checked in Section~\ref{dev:bell}. The product-diagonal construction remains valid; \citet[section~4]{powers1967representations} treats product-state representations but does not supply the false general implication.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: False without the missing nondegeneracy or another hypothesis ensuring a product eigenbasis; it is not an open problem.

title: Consistent eigenvalue tables and the infinite product probability space
notes: The sums \(\sum_{\alpha_n}\mu(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)=\mu(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_{n-1})\) define a cylinder measure on \(\prod_i\mathbf Z_2\); Haar measure is an example.
statement: When a fixed product basis really diagonalizes the densities, partial traces give consistent finite probability tables. The resulting Borel probability measure on \(\{0,1\}^{\mathbf Z}\) is unique. The product of equal weights is the Haar probability measure on the compact product group \(\prod_{i\in\mathbf Z}\mathbf Z/2\mathbf Z\).
fate: This is the valid classical part of 1970-195.3. For the Haar example the corresponding quantum state is tracial, so \citet[section~4]{powers1967representations} identifies a type \(\mathrm{II}_1\), rather than type III, factor.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: GNS representation and the role of type III factors
notes: The positive form, quotient, completion, and left multiplication are repeated, followed by the statement that type III factors are important.
statement: The GNS construction in 1970-195.7 applies to all these states. The study of type III factors motivates selecting nontracial infinite product and Gibbs states; it does not classify every state constructed on P000312--313 as type III.
fate: \citet[section~4]{powers1967representations} constructs type III product-state factors and distinguishes the pure and tracial endpoints. This supplies the prior mathematical background without converting a motivational remark into a universal theorem.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: The category of ordered four-subspace systems
notes: \(S=(P;E_1,E_2,E_3,E_4)\), with ordered subspaces and morphisms carrying each \(E_i\) into its counterpart; direct sums and permutations are introduced.
statement: Objects consist of a finite-dimensional vector space \(P\) over \(k\) and four ordered subspaces. A morphism \(u:S\to S^{\prime}\) satisfies \(u(E_i)\subset E_i^{\prime}\); an isomorphism is an invertible \(u\) carrying each subspace onto the corresponding subspace. Direct sums are componentwise. Permuting labels is a separate action, not part of ordered isomorphism.
fate: Exactly \citet[section~1, p.~762]{gelfandponomarev1971quadruples}. The announcement was received 21 October 1970 and printed in 1971.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: The four-armed quiver and its injectivity condition
notes: The category is said to be equivalent to diagrams with four arrows directed into one central vertex.
statement: Four-subspace systems identify with representations of the inward-oriented affine \(D_4\) quiver in which all four arrow maps are injective. Arbitrary representations also include kernels at outer vertices and hence are not literally the same category. The diagrammatic language unifies several matrix classification problems.
reconstruction: Injectivity of the four arrows is supplied; it is forced by calling their domains subspaces.
fate: The subsequent quiver framework is explicit in \citet[introduction and final example]{bernsteingelfandponomarev1973coxeter}; compare \citet[section~1]{gelfandponomarev1971quadruples}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: Encoding similarity of an operator by four subspaces
notes: In \(E\oplus E\), take the two coordinate summands, the graph of \(A:E\to E\), and the diagonal.
statement: The quadruple \(S_A=(E\oplus E;E\oplus0,0\oplus E,\operatorname{graph}A,\Delta_E)\) is isomorphic to \(S_B\) exactly when \(A\) and \(B\) are similar. The first two subspaces force a block diagonal map and the diagonal forces the two blocks to agree. Direct sum and indecomposability correspond to those of operators.
fate: The identical construction is \citet[section~1, example~1]{gelfandponomarev1971quadruples}; the equivalence is also stated in \citet[p.~2]{enomotowatatani2004subspaces}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: Opposite maps, matrix pencils, and linear relations
notes: The notes mention \(A:E\to F\), \(B:F\to E\), Kronecker's problem, and relations regarded as arbitrary graphs.
statement: In \(E\oplus F\), take the two coordinate subspaces together with \(\{(x,Ax)\}\) and \(\{(By,y)\}\). Two parallel maps \(E\to F\) instead give two ordinary graphs and encode a matrix pencil. Replacing graphs by arbitrary subspaces of \(E\oplus F\) encodes linear relations; a relation need not be the graph of a single-valued map.
reconstruction: The three related encodings are written separately rather than treating the word graph as imposing single-valuedness.
fate: These are exactly the five examples in \citet[section~1, pp.~762--763; section~4]{gelfandponomarev1971quadruples}. The article explains that the four-subspace problem includes, but is broader than, pairs of linear relations.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: Four lines and the cross-ratio parameter
notes: Four lines in a plane have one invariant \(\lambda\), with its transformations under relabeling.
statement: For four distinct ordered lines in a two-dimensional vector space over an algebraically closed field, normalize three projective points to \(0,1,\infty\). The fourth gives \(\lambda\notin\{0,1\}\). Relabeling gives the six values \(\lambda,1-\lambda,1/\lambda,1/(1-\lambda),\lambda/(\lambda-1),(\lambda-1)/\lambda\), with coincidences at special values.
fate: This is the \(k=1\) parameter family in \citet[section~2]{gelfandponomarev1971quadruples}. The P000316 list, and even the compressed list in the announcement, omit one of the six cross-ratio transforms; the earlier P000314 generators recover it.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: Indecomposable classification and the five possible defects
notes: Every system decomposes into indecomposables of defect \(0,\pm1,\pm2\); the boxed definition is \(2\dim P-\sum_i\dim E_i\).
statement: Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, every finite four-subspace system is a direct sum of the canonical indecomposables in the Gelfand--Ponomarev list. With the published convention \(\delta(S)=\sum_i\dim E_i-2\dim P\), indecomposable defects belong to \(\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\). The notebook's boxed definition is \(-\delta\), while its subsequent labels use \(\delta\).
fate: \citet[Claims~1--2 and Theorem~1, pp.~764--765]{gelfandponomarev1971quadruples} gives the classification; \citet[Theorems~9.1--9.2]{enomotowatatani2004subspaces} reproduces the complete list. The original received date is before this lecture, but printing is 1971.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Classified; the defect sign must be normalized before using the listed labels.

title: The two even-dimensional defect-one normal forms
notes: For \(P=\langle e_1,\ldots,e_k,f_1,\ldots,f_k\rangle\), the first system has \(E_3=\langle e_2+f_1,\ldots,e_k+f_{k-1}\rangle\); the second adjoins \(e_1,f_k\).
statement: In both forms \(E_1=\langle e_i\rangle\), \(E_2=\langle f_i\rangle\), and \(E_4=\langle e_i+f_i\rangle\). The first has \(\dim E_3=k-1\) and published defect \(-1\), the second \(\dim E_3=k+1\) and defect \(+1\). Label permutations give the other distinguished-index forms.
fate: The displayed bases match \citet[section~2, p.~763]{gelfandponomarev1971quadruples}. Only the notebook's preceding definition reverses the defect sign.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: The exceptional and one-parameter even-dimensional defect-zero forms
notes: One form takes \(E_3=\langle e_1,e_2+f_1,\ldots,e_k+f_{k-1}\rangle\); the other has a Jordan-chain parameter \(\lambda\ne0,1\).
statement: Keep \(E_1,E_2,E_4\) as in 1970-198.7. The exceptional form has the stated \(E_3\); its permutations give \(S_{i,j}(2k,0)\). The family \(S(2k,0;\lambda)\) has \(E_3=\langle e_1+\lambda f_1,e_2+f_1+\lambda f_2,\ldots,e_k+f_{k-1}+\lambda f_k\rangle\), \(\lambda\in k\setminus\{0,1\}\). The excluded parameters belong to exceptional label families, not to additional generic families.
fate: \citet[section~2, p.~763 and Claim~1]{gelfandponomarev1971quadruples} gives these exact forms and their permutation rules.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: Odd-dimensional defect-two forms and duality
notes: The notes write \(S(2k-1,2)\) explicitly and obtain \(S(2k-1,-2)\) by taking orthogonals.
statement: For \(k\geq2\), in dimension \(2k-1\), the displayed four subspaces each have dimension \(k\), so their published defect is \(+2\). Their annihilators in \(P^*\) have dimension \(k-1\), hence defect \(-2\). Dual annihilators are the field-independent meaning of orthogonals; a chosen inner product may identify them with orthogonal complements. The one-dimensional endpoints are handled separately.
fate: The bases coincide with \citet[section~2, p.~764]{gelfandponomarev1971quadruples}; see also \citet[section~9, forms~8--9]{enomotowatatani2004subspaces}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: The notebook incorrectly excludes odd-dimensional defect zero
notes: \ru{def 0 в неч.-мерном не бывает.}
statement: Odd-dimensional indecomposables of defect zero do exist. For example \((k;k,0,k,0)\) in ambient dimension one is indecomposable and has defect zero. More generally the published list contains \(S_{i,j}(2k-1,0)\). The manuscript omits these forms, together with its full odd-dimensional defect-one list.
fate: \citet[Claim~2, p.~764]{gelfandponomarev1971quadruples} explicitly includes the missing odd families. The counterexample follows directly from the definition, with no unresolved classification issue.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: The literal exclusion is false; the published classification supplies the omitted families.

title: Parameters and local rigidity are not interchangeable
notes: General-position systems are said to have no parameter; parameter-free indecomposables are said always to be stable under deformation.
statement: For fixed dimensions, local rigidity means that the \(\mathrm{GL}(P)\)-orbit is open in the product of Grassmannians. Four distinct lines in a plane form a general-position family with varying cross ratio. A finite exceptional list does not by itself imply open orbits: exceptional defect-zero systems can deform into the parameter family.
fate: The explicit families and exceptional specializations in \citet[section~2]{gelfandponomarev1971quadruples} already disprove the unrestricted parameter/general-position slogan. The regular-versus-irregular distinction in \citet[final example]{bernsteingelfandponomarev1973coxeter} is the appropriate later framework; it does not identify every parameter-free case as rigid.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: False in the stated generality; rigidity requires an orbit or deformation calculation.

title: A direct sum of rigid systems need not be rigid
notes: \(S(5,2)\) and \(S(1,2)\) are called stable, but their sum deforms to \(S(3,2)\oplus S(3,2)\); a simple proof is requested.
statement: Using the published defect convention, all three terms are the defect-two canonical systems; both sums have ambient dimension six and four subspaces of dimension four. The intended assertion is that arbitrarily small deformations of \(S(5,2)\oplus S(1,2)\) have the isomorphism type \(S(3,2)^{\oplus2}\). Thus the latter is the generic nearby orbit; the former lies in its orbit closure.
reconstruction: Work over \(\mathbf C\) with ordered subspaces and analytic deformations in the product of Grassmannians. The supplied proof is independently checked reconstruction, not a claim of historical novelty.
fate: The canonical systems are exactly those of \citet[section~2]{gelfandponomarev1971quadruples}. The opened classification texts did not locate this precise degeneration. Section~\ref{dev:four-subspaces} proves it: \(\operatorname{End}S(3,2)=\mathbf C\), so the orbit of \(S(3,2)^{\oplus2}\) has dimension \(36-4=32=\dim\operatorname{Gr}(4,6)^4\) and is open dense. A generic line in a Grassmann chart through the special sum supplies an analytic family. Class C here records the partial historical literature match followed by a completed bounded development, not present mathematical openness.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: the precise deformation over the complex numbers is proved in this chapter. No mathematical obstruction remains for this bounded question; only the exact historical publication of its elementary proof was not verified.
worth: Worth a bounded reconstruction: an orbit-dimension argument gives the requested elementary deformation proof, while the exact historical attribution remains unverified.

title: Uniqueness of decomposition into indecomposables
notes: The last parenthesis says that decomposition is unique if the indecomposables are distinct and that the number is always the same.
statement: The finite-dimensional category has the Krull--Schmidt property: the multiset of indecomposable isomorphism classes, with multiplicities, is unique up to permutation. Distinctness of summands is unnecessary. Existence follows by decreasing ambient dimension; uniqueness uses finite-dimensional endomorphism algebras and the usual local-endomorphism argument.
fate: The direct-sum classification in \citet[Theorem~1]{gelfandponomarev1971quadruples}, viewed in the representation category of \citet{bernsteingelfandponomarev1973coxeter}, is a classical Krull--Schmidt setting.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: Decomposing a Čech cocycle into pieces with a local primitive
notes: Write \(m_{ij}=\sum_km_{ij}^{(k)}\), with \(m_{ik}^{(k)}\in M_{f_i}\) and the cocycle identity already valid in \(M_{f_if_j}\).
statement: For a finite distinguished-open cover, choose \(N\) and lifts \(u_i^{(k)}\in M_{f_i}\) of \(f_k^N m_{ik}\). Increase the common exponent, multiplying the lifts by the same extra powers of \(f_k\), so that all finitely many localization-equality errors vanish and \(u_i^{(k)}-u_j^{(k)}=f_k^N m_{ij}\) in \(M_{f_if_j}\). Choose \(g_k\in A\) with \(\sum_k g_kf_k^N=1\). Then \(n_i=\sum_k g_ku_i^{(k)}\) satisfies \(m_{ij}=n_i-n_j\), proving degree-one affine acyclicity. The lifts are chosen; localization maps need not be injective.
fate: This corrects the proof attempt of record 196 and agrees with the localization argument of \citet[Lemma~30.2.1]{stacks2026affine}. The first one-index trial on P000317 has a sign slip; the final P000318 formula has the consistent sign.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: The sheaf of units is not a quasi-coherent module sheaf
notes: \(\mathcal O^*(U)\) consists of functions avoiding all primes of \(U\), and is called a subsheaf of the structure sheaf.
statement: \(\mathcal O_X^\times\) is the sheaf of invertible regular functions under multiplication. It is a subsheaf of sets and an abelian sheaf under that law, but not an \(\mathcal O_X\)-submodule: zero is not a unit and units are not closed under addition. Affine acyclicity for quasi-coherent modules therefore does not apply to it.
fate: The Picard-group interpretation used in \citet[section~59.69]{stacks2026picardcurves} provides the relevant cohomology. The different algebraic structures are essential to the next exercise.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: Nonzero first cohomology of units on a punctured elliptic curve
notes: For \(A=\mathbf C[x,y]/(y^2-x^3+1)\), prove \(H^1(\operatorname{Spec}A,\mathcal O^*)\ne0\).
statement: Let \(E\) be the smooth projective completion of \(y^2=x^3-1\), with point at infinity \(O\), and \(U=E\setminus\{O\}\). Then \(H^1_{\mathrm{Zar}}(U,\mathcal O_U^\times)=\operatorname{Pic}(U)\cong\operatorname{Pic}(E)/\mathbf Z[O]\cong\operatorname{Pic}^0(E)\cong E(\mathbf C)\), which is nonzero.
fate: \citet[proof of Lemma~59.69.3]{stacks2026picardcurves} gives the quotient by removed-point classes. Together with the degree decomposition for a pointed elliptic curve, this solves the notebook exercise. No claim that an arbitrary topological torus has this sheaf cohomology is intended.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: A solved standard exercise; affine quasi-coherent vanishing does not cover the multiplicative unit sheaf.

title: Cohomology of punctured affine space
notes: For \(S=\mathbf A^n\setminus\{0\}\), only degrees zero and \(n-1\) can be nonzero, and the latter is infinite-dimensional.
statement: Over a field \(k\), for \(n\geq2\), \(H^0(S,\mathcal O)=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), \(H^q(S,\mathcal O)=0\) for \(q\notin\{0,n-1\}\), and \(H^{n-1}\) is freely spanned over \(k\) by monomials \(x_1^{-a_1}\cdots x_n^{-a_n}\), all \(a_i\geq1\). For \(n=1\), \(H^0=k[x,x^{-1}]\) instead.
fate: The detailed calculation is carried out in record 201. It is the localization-complex calculation underlying \citet[Lemma~30.8.1]{stacks2026projective}; the affine-cover acyclicity needed for it is \citet[Lemma~30.2.2]{stacks2026affine}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: Deligne's logarithmic de Rham description of an open variety
notes: A complete smooth \(X\), a transversal codimension-one boundary \(Y\), and local forms \(df/f\) are described; resolution reduces to this situation and the cohomology ring is said to be independent of the resolution.
statement: For a smooth complex algebraic variety \(U\), choose a smooth proper compactification \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\) whose reduced boundary \(D=X\setminus U\) is a simple normal-crossings divisor. Then \(\Omega_X^\bullet(\log D)\) computes \(H^*(U^{\mathrm{an}},\mathbf C)\) by hypercohomology, compatibly with products. The resulting cohomology and the mixed Hodge structure do not depend on the chosen such compactification. Smoothness, characteristic zero, and normal crossings are necessary parts of this formulation.
reconstruction: Hypercohomology, the smooth open variety, and the precise normal-crossings condition replace the compressed word ring. The mixed-Hodge statement is additional published context, not words attributed to the notebook.
fate: \citet[Proposition~3.1.8 and Theorem~3.2.5]{deligne1971hodge} supplies the comparison and independence. The paper was received 15 September 1970 and printed in 1971. The notebook already reports it as Deligne's theorem; the submission date is not treated as a public-release date.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established; the notebook records an already circulating theorem, with the first printing checked here in 1971.
speaker: Unattributed report of P. Deligne's theorem

title: The uniform relative-commutant criterion for a factor state
notes: The displayed theorem says \(\forall x\,\forall\varepsilon>0\,\exists y\) satisfying the correlation estimate, with \(y\) in a local commutant.
statement: For a state \(\varphi\) of the spin UHF algebra, \(M_\varphi\) is a factor if and only if for every \(x\in\mathcal A\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(n\) such that \[|\varphi(xy)-\varphi(x)\varphi(y)|\leq\varepsilon\|y\|\quad\text{for all }y\in\mathcal A([-n,n])^{\prime}\cap\mathcal A.\] The quantifier is over every element of the tail relative commutant, not one chosen \(y\).
reconstruction: The manuscript quantifier is emended to the uniform relative-commutant condition in Powers; the reconstruction is mathematically necessary because the literal condition is vacuous.
fate: \citet[Theorem~2.5 and proof; Russian translation pp.~100--101]{powers1967representations} gives this criterion, after rescaling \(x\) to incorporate \(\varepsilon\). The original theorem is 1967; the Russian translation available to the seminar is 1969.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the corrected uniform quantifiers. The literal existential condition is vacuous because \(y=0\) always works.

title: The classical tail-independence form of the criterion
notes: For measure-type states the estimate becomes \(\sup_B|\mu(A\cap B)-\mu(A)\mu(B)|\to0\).
statement: For the product-diagonal states of 1970-195.3, the equivalent classical condition is: for every fixed cylinder event \(A\), \[\sup_{B\in\sigma(\omega_j:|j|>n)}|\mu(A\cap B)-\mu(A)\mu(B)|\longrightarrow0.\] Uniformity in the distant event is required. For a two-sided lattice, outside \([-n,n]\) replaces a one-sided first-\(n\)-coordinates description.
reconstruction: The two-sided tail sigma-field and the fixed-cylinder quantifier are made explicit; the notebook's measure terminology is not used to bypass its diagonalization error.
fate: This follows by restricting the correlation criterion of \citet[Theorem~2.5]{powers1967representations} to diagonal projections and extending by simple-function approximation. It applies to the genuinely product-diagonal construction, not automatically to the weaker commuting-density definition of record 197.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: Product states satisfy the factor criterion
notes: Product measures with site probabilities bounded below by a fixed \(c>0\) are given as examples.
statement: Every infinite product state of the tensor-product matrix algebra is a factor state. The lower bound on site probabilities in the notebook is sufficient but unnecessary; pure site states are allowed as well. For an observable supported in \([-n,n]\), correlation with the outside algebra factorizes exactly, and norm approximation handles quasi-local observables.
fate: \citet[Lemma~4.1, Russian translation p.~113]{powers1967representations} proves the product-state assertion. Section~4 distinguishes type I, tracial type \(\mathrm{II}_1\), and nontracial type III examples.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: The finite-temperature one-dimensional Gibbs state is primary
notes: The last line says that the state obtained from the Hamiltonian is a factor.
statement: For the self-adjoint finite-range one-dimensional interaction and finite-temperature Gibbs limit of 1970-195.4--5, the GNS von Neumann algebra is a factor. This conclusion does not assert that all states of the algebra, or all infinite-volume Gibbs states in higher dimensions, are factors.
fate: The primary-state conclusion is explicitly in the abstract of \citet{araki1969gibbs}. The notebook is reporting a known result within the stated spin-chain setup.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: The principal-open cover of punctured affine space
notes: \(X=\operatorname{Spec}A[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\setminus\{0\}\) is covered by the \(X_i\) where \(x_i\ne0\).
statement: Put \(R=A[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), \(I=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\), and \(U=\operatorname{Spec}R\setminus V(I)\). Over a general base ring, \(V(I)\cong\operatorname{Spec}A\) is the zero section, not a single point. The cover is \(D(x_i)\), with sections \(R_{x_i}\); every intersection inverts all corresponding variables.
reconstruction: The zero-section notation makes explicit the set of containing prime ideals already specified in the source on P320.
fate: The localization cover and its cohomology computation are the same monomial complex used in \citet[Lemma~30.8.1]{stacks2026projective}, justified by \citet[Lemma~30.2.2]{stacks2026affine}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: Global functions extend across the zero section in dimension at least two
notes: The notes identify \(H^0\) with the polynomial ring and explicitly exclude \(n=1\) in the preliminary calculation.
statement: For every commutative ring \(A\) and \(n\geq2\), \(\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)=A[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\). For \(n=1\), \(U=D(x_1)\) and the answer is \(A[x_1,x_1^{-1}]\). The polynomial-extension statement follows by intersecting the relevant Laurent subrings, or by monomial Čech exactness.
fate: The affine-cover proof is classical; the graded version is computed in \citet[proof of Lemma~30.8.1]{stacks2026projective}. This continues the earlier punctured-affine examples listed as 1965-58.7 and affine-cover methods 1965-70.6.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: The three-variable one-cocycle calculation is a Koszul syzygy
notes: The \(n=3\) calculation clears denominators and separates polynomial multiples of powers of the coordinates.
statement: The sequence \(x_1^N,\ldots,x_n^N\) is regular in \(A[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) for every \(N\geq1\), even when \(A\) has zero divisors. Its Koszul complex is exact away from degree zero. Thus a relation among the powered coordinates is generated by the elementary skew relations; after localization this gives the required Čech primitive. In three variables it proves \(H^1(U,\mathcal O)=0\).
reconstruction: The regular-sequence statement is supplied as a precise modern formulation of the polynomial-divisibility argument.
fate: The notebook announces the Koszul complex as the next language for this calculation. The monomial proof in \citet[proof of Lemma~30.8.1]{stacks2026projective} verifies the same vanishing without depending on the inconsistent intermediate polynomial subscripts.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: Vanishing in all intermediate degrees
notes: The argument for \(H^1\) is extended to \(H^q\), except the last possible degree.
statement: For \(n\geq2\), \(H^q(U,\mathcal O_U)=0\) when \(1\leq q\leq n-2\); it is also zero for \(q\geq n\) because the cover has \(n\) members. Splitting the Čech complex by Laurent monomials gives a simplex complex unless every coordinate has negative exponent, which contributes only in degree \(n-1\).
fate: This is the ungraded version of \citet[proof of Lemma~30.8.1]{stacks2026projective}. The complete list of nonzero degrees agrees with the preliminary announcement in record 199.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: The top cohomology as negative Laurent monomials
notes: Top cohomology consists of negative powers of every variable; multiplication by polynomials is followed by throwing away terms with nonnegative powers.
statement: For \(n\geq2\), \[H^{n-1}(U,\mathcal O_U)\cong R_{x_1\cdots x_n}\big/\sum_iR_{x_1\cdots\widehat{x_i}\cdots x_n}\cong\bigoplus_{a_1,\ldots,a_n\geq1}A\,x_1^{-a_1}\cdots x_n^{-a_n}.\] The quotient, not ordinary Laurent multiplication alone, determines its \(R\)-module action.
fate: \citet[Lemma~30.8.1 and its monomial proof]{stacks2026projective} gives the homogeneous pieces of this module. Over a nonzero field it is infinite-dimensional. The case \(n=1\) belongs to degree-zero global sections and must be kept separate.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: Residue pairing with the restricted linear dual
notes: \(H^{n-1}=\operatorname{Hom}_{R}(R,k)\) is written twice, with \(k\) the evaluation-at-zero module; the proposed pairing takes the coefficient of \((x_1\cdots x_n)^{-1}\).
statement: For \(n\geq2\), over a field \(k\), the pairing \(\langle f,\eta\rangle=\operatorname{coeff}_{x_1^{-1}\cdots x_n^{-1}}(f\eta)\) is nondegenerate and identifies top cohomology with the finite-support, or graded restricted, \(k\)-linear dual \(R^\circ=\bigoplus_{d\geq0}\operatorname{Hom}_k(R_d,k)\), where \(\operatorname{Hom}_k(R_d,k)\) is placed in degree \(-d-n\). Its \(R\)-action is \((r\ell)(f)=\ell(rf)\). It is neither \(\operatorname{Hom}_R(R,k)\cong k\) nor the full algebraic dual \(\prod_d\operatorname{Hom}_k(R_d,k)\).
reconstruction: The incorrect ring-linear Hom is replaced by the restricted linear dual detected directly by the displayed coefficient-extraction pairing; \(n\geq2\) is explicit.
fate: The monomial bases in \citet[Lemma~30.8.1]{stacks2026projective} verify the pairing term by term. The source's reference to Serre duality is a thematic link: this affine local-duality calculation needs the restricted dual and the differential/degree convention stated here.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: The corrected residue-dual identification is established. The displayed \(R\)-linear Hom has the wrong dimension and action.

title: General base-ring version and the limits of the duality slogan
notes: The theorem is restated with coefficient ring \(A\), writing \(H^{n-1}=\operatorname{Hom}_{H^0}(H^0,A)\).
statement: The Laurent-quotient and direct-sum description in 1970-201.5 works for every commutative \(A\). Each homogeneous polynomial piece \(R_d\) is finite free, so coefficient extraction gives the corresponding restricted \(A\)-linear dual. The general-base statement does not turn this into an \(R\)-linear Hom to the evaluation-at-zero module.
reconstruction: The same correction is made over the coefficient ring, using finite free homogeneous polynomial pieces instead of a field-only argument.
fate: The arbitrary-ring computation is explicitly allowed in \citet[Lemma~30.8.1]{stacks2026projective}. No field-only dimension argument is used to justify extension of the Laurent formula to general \(A\).
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the hypotheses in the statement.

title: Commuting operators and the announced Koszul complex
notes: The notes briefly connect the calculation with several commuting operators and promise the Koszul complex next time.
